new_statements.quote: Betonung. Die Betonung erfolgt mit wenigen Ausnahmen, die im Wortregister durch Akzente gekennzeichnet sind, auf der vorletzten Silbe. Hiebei sind auch die echten Diphthonge als zweisilbig anzusehen. Ausnahmen: lífaja Schmetterling, láhua Asche, búea Leguan, ámuni jener. Die enklitischen Possess.-Pronomina und das Pluralsuffix re haben keinen Einfluß auf die Betonung. Man sagt also: háta-re, íma-re, tína-ku.
new_statements.translation: Stress. With few exceptions, which are marked by accents in the word list, stress falls on the penultimate syllable. Here the true diphthongs are also to be treated as disyllabic. Exceptions: lífaja 'butterfly', láhua 'ash', búea 'monitor lizard', ámuni 'that one'. The enclitic possessive pronouns and the plural suffix re have no influence on the stress. Thus one says: háta-re, íma-re, tína-ku.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the stem; the true diphthongs a͜i and a͜u count as two syllables for this purpose (so a final diphthong takes stress on its first element); enclitic possessive pronouns and the plural suffix -re lie outside the stress domain, so the stem keeps its penultimate stress (háta-re, tína-ku). Stems are almost always disyllabic and vowel-final (same page), so the rule mostly yields initial stress on bare stems.
new_statements.exceptions: A few lexical exceptions marked with accents in the word list, all with antepenultimate (initial) stress: lífaja 'butterfly', láhua 'ash', búea 'monitor lizard', ámuni 'that one'.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level stress on the lexical stem; enclitics (possessive pronouns, plural -re) are excluded from the domain. Description of Tauern's 'Wahinama-Sprache', which he equates with the Manusela language (his 1928 introduction calls it 'Manusela-Sprache'; material collected mainly in Manusela village, spoken from the Wai Samal to the Sapolewa, mountains to north coast, plus Hatita and Selamena south of the range). Data from the 1910s, published posthumously 1931; accent readings on the four exceptions checked by eye on the page image.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted source describes Tauern's 'Wahinama-Sprache', which is Manusela itself, not a different language: Tauern's 1928 introduction (Anthropos 23:1001) lists the same material as the 'Manusela-Sprache' (spoken north of the central range between the Salawei and Samal rivers, plus Teluti Bay villages), the 1931 section says the material was gathered mainly in Manusela village, Glottolog lists Wahinama and Wahai as alternative names of manu1258, and Loski & Loski 1989:120 call Tauern's Wahinama 'a Manusela dialect'. The variety is thus the Manusela-village / northern (Kanikeh-area) dialect of the chain; Loski & Loski 1989 distinguish five dialects (South Manusela, Maneo, Huaulu, Hatuolu, Kanikeh), of which Huaulu has its own code (huau1237, hud), and Grimes & Edwards 2026 give ~71% average lexical similarity across the chain. ISO 639-3 renamed wha 'Sou Upaa' in 2016.
